questions.prompt: With `arr = [1, 2, 2, 2, 3]` and `target = 2`, what do `LowerBound(arr, 2)` and `UpperBound(arr, 2)` return?
options: 1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 4
0 and 4
questions.explanation: Lower bound is the first index with `arr[i] >= 2` (index 1); upper bound is the first index with `arr[i] > 2` (index 4).

questions.prompt: Using the two bound functions, how do you get the **count** of `target` and its **last** index in a sorted array with duplicates?
options: Count = `UpperBound`; last index = `LowerBound - 1`
Count = `UpperBound + LowerBound`; last index = `UpperBound`
Count = `LowerBound - UpperBound`; last index = `LowerBound + 1`
Count = `UpperBound - LowerBound`; last index = `UpperBound - 1`
questions.explanation: Upper bound is one past the last match and lower bound is the first match, so their difference is the count and `UpperBound(target) - 1` is the last occurrence.

questions.prompt: Why does the binary search compute `mid` as `left + (right - left) / 2` instead of `(left + right) / 2`?
options: It rounds up instead of down, so the loop always ends
For huge indices `left + right` can overflow `int` and go negative
It is required for the recursive version only
It makes the search O(1) in the best case
questions.explanation: Both give the same middle for small values, but `left + right` can overflow for very large indices; `left + (right - left) / 2` never exceeds `right`.

questions.prompt: Why is binary search a poor fit for a linked list, even a sorted one?
options: Linked lists cannot hold duplicate values
It only works on arrays of `int`
It needs random access to jump to the middle element
Linked lists are always unsorted
questions.explanation: Binary search needs to reach the middle element directly; a linked list can only be walked node by node.

questions.prompt: When is linear search the right choice?
options: When the data is unsorted, `n` is very small, or you only search once
When you will run many repeated queries over a large array
Only when the array is sorted
Never; binary search is always faster
questions.explanation: Linear search works on any collection without sorting and is the fastest option for very small `n` or a one-time search; it is too slow for large data or repeated queries.
